description: Find real parts by description. Returns part numbers with their footprint, height and the colours they were really made in. Use this instead of guessing a part number. Printed parts are found by what is on them with the word print: "porsche print", "control panel print", "3623 print" (3623's prints); a part with a sticker on, with sticker.
name: search_parts

description: Check a list of parts for overlaps, floating parts and whether it is one connected model, and weigh it: whether it stands (its centre of mass against the edge of what it stands on, in every pose its hinges and turntables reach), the counterweight that would hold it, and its most loaded stud joints. Safe to call on a partial design while you work.

face.description: which way the studs point. Omit for up.

rot.description: quarter turns about the face direction, 0-3

section.description: the section this brick belongs to, if any. Its x, y and z are then that section's own coordinates, not the model's.

x.description: studs across, to the low corner. Tenths allowed.

y.description: plates up from the ground, to the low corner. Quarters allowed, for parts lying on their side.

z.description: studs deep, to the low corner. Tenths allowed.

about.description: mirror: which way the line runs

at.description: mirror: the line to reflect about, in studs. fill, round: where the footprint's low corner sits, as {x, y, z} (a round lying along x or z: the low end of it, on the ground).

axis.description: round: y stands it up (the default); x or z lays it along that axis on the ground — a boiler, a fuselage, a hull, a log

band_color.description: fill with rise 3, prism: a course in this colour every eight, a string course where a storey's ledge is. A black wall gets dark bluish grey bands unless mix_color or this says otherwise.

bands.description: shape: [{"from": plates, "to": plates, "color"}] — a waterline, a stripe, a belly, by height.

beside.description: round: more rounds standing round this one, touching it, pinned where their Technic courses meet (start both stacks the same, each with a technic course at one height): {"count": 2 or 4, "diameter", "color", "stack"}. Boosters on a core, twin funnels, a cluster of silos.

box.description: shape: {"from": [x, y, z], "size": [across, plates up, deep], "round": studs its plan corners are rounded by, "chamfer": studs they are cut by, "edge": studs its top edges are rounded by}.

bricks.description: repeat: what to repeat. mirror: what to reflect, if not everything so far.

face.description: which way the studs point. Omit for up.

rot.description: quarter turns about the face direction, 0-3

section.description: the section this brick belongs to, if any. Its x, y and z are then that section's own coordinates, not the model's.

x.description: studs across, to the low corner. Tenths allowed.

y.description: plates up from the ground, to the low corner. Quarters allowed, for parts lying on their side.

z.description: studs deep, to the low corner. Tenths allowed.

color.description: fill, rock: the colour (rock: 72 if not said)

courses.description: studs_out: how many rows, each four plates tall; prism: how many courses of bricks, three plates each (with piers, left out for a display model's proportions, 3.3 times as tall as wide)

cuts.description: shape: solids taken away, said the same way: a cockpit, a doorway; "keep": true keeps the cut clear of every part.

diameter.description: round: studs across — the sizes round parts come in (at is the low corner of its square)

dome.description: shape: an ellipsoid's top half, said the same way.

door.description: prism: an arched door at the foot of the face looking +z, two studs wide and six courses tall, for a stair to lead up to; true unless said with piers, false unless said without

dress.description: studs_out: what every side stud carries — a mix (the default), flat tiles for a smooth panel, round plates as rivets, round tiles as portholes, or lights (round tiles in a transparent face_color): a band of detail along a hull, a boiler, a wall

edge_color.description: fill: a second colour for the outside stud of every layer — hull plating, a trim, a kerb.

ellipsoid.description: shape: {"centre": [x, y, z], "radii": [studs across, plates up, studs deep]}.

extrude.description: shape: {"along": "x" or "z", "from": studs across, "width": studs, "profile": [[studs along, plates up], ...] its top seen from the side, "under": the same for its underside (0 unless said), "round": studs its top edges are rounded by}.

face.description: shape: a face laid on a curved side, studs out — {"facing": "+z", "x", "y", "z": its middle, "across": 4, 6 or 8, "color": the disc, "rim": the plate behind it, "eyes": the iris, "beak": its colour or -1}: a round plate disc on side studs, two 2 x 2 round eyes with printed eye tiles, a beak.

face_color.description: studs_out: the colour of what is laid on the side studs

facing.description: studs_out: which way the face looks

layers.description: fill: how many of the footprint, stacked up

loft.description: shape: {"along": "x" or "z", "centre": studs across (half the widest unless said), "sections": [{"at": studs along, "width": studs, "height": plates, "bottom": plates, "round": 0 a box to 1 an ellipse, "keel": 0 to 1, how far its lower half narrows to a V, "offset": studs across}, ...]} — the section between each two is in between; width 0 at an end is a point.

masonry.description: fill: the share of its 1x2 and 1x4 bricks laid as masonry bricks (98283, 15533), stonework facing away from the middle, 0 to 1. For a wall one stud thick.

mix.description: fill: the share in mix_color, up to 0.5; 0.15 if not said.

mix_color.description: fill, rock: a second colour through some of its bricks, chosen by where they are, the same every time — a weathered wall. Real castle walls are 9-19% their second grey.

open.description: prism: faces left out at the back, so the rooms inside show; with piers, any number opens the core's whole back, the piers there left closed

panels.description: shape: its straight sides as tiles on bricks with side studs every other course (true, the default), or plain bricks (false).

pattern.description: repeat: the bricks again, stepped each time. mirror: everything so far, reflected about a line — build one side and mirror it rather than writing both. fill: a footprint tiled with the largest plates that fit, or with rise 3 a wall of short bricks in a running bond — and with layers, a shrink and a wall it is a dome, a cone, a hull, a tube or a bowl in one object. rock: a crag in one object — courses stepping in unevenly towards a peak off the middle, faced with slopes, cheese slopes, pebbles and bare ledges in two greys; a different seed is a different rock. studs_out: a face built sideways in one object — courses of 1x1 bricks with a side stud, tied by plates, each stud carrying a tile, round tile, round plate or cheese slope laid on its side; the arithmetic of where a side stud is, done for you. prism: a many-sided shaft in one object — a tower, a pier, a turret of 5 to 16 sides, each face a bonded wall turned to its angle about the middle (at is the middle), grooved where the faces meet. round: anything round in section, in one object — a column, a rocket stage, a lighthouse, a silo, a boiler, a fuselage, a tree trunk — of the round parts sets use at each diameter (round bricks, cylinder halves, corner rounds tied by round plates), colour bands, cones, Technic struts and spokes up its stack, ending in a nose; upright or lying along x or z. shape: a body that is not a box, said as solids — a loft through cross-sections, an extruded side profile, a revolve, a box with rounded or cut corners and edges, an ellipsoid or dome — less any cuts, laid in the parts a builder would choose: bricks and plates inside, slopes and curved slopes fitted to the surface's fall, inverted slopes under it, wedge plates on a diagonal edge, round parts where a section is round, a side that curves up and down laid on its side on side studs, tiles on top, one half and its mirror; a car's body, a hull, a fuselage, an animal's body. Another shape standing on it keeps its studs there.

piers.description: prism: faceted piers clustered round it, each a prism of its own built against the core, with a cleft between each two — a tower like Orthanc in one object. The core is capped with a summit two plates thick at y + 3 x courses, and piers taller than the core rise past it as horns: blades of plates on their side, cut by wedge plates, sweeping out and back in to a point (the reply says where the tips are).

courses.description: how tall, in courses of three plates; more than the core's for horns (a fifth more; a blade rises at least two and a half times its width)

flare.description: blade: studs its sweep reaches out (half its width)

horns.description: what piers taller than the core rise into: a blade (the default, as set 10237 builds Orthanc's), a square spire stepping in to a point, or flat, a turret's cap

out.description: studs from the core's middle to each pier's (set into the core by its wall's thickness)

radius.description: studs from a pier's middle to the outside of its faces (two thirds of the core's; smaller than keeps faces two studs wide at its sides, it is laid at that and said)

turn.description: degrees round from +z to the first pier (between two faces, so there is a cleft front and back)

plinth.description: prism: {"steps": 1 to 4, "out": studs, "stair": true, "rock": true} — the tower raised on square terraces stepping down from its foot, two courses each, their tops tiled in the second tone up to its faces, with a stair cut into the front (+z) up to its door's level, and crags in its dark tones rising against it at their corners and sides (rock: false for none). The reply says the tower's foot (and add_rooms' y).

radius.description: prism: studs from the middle to the outside of a face

revolve.description: shape: {"axis": "y", "x" or "z", "centre": [x, y, z], "profile": [[along it (plates up y, studs along x or z), radius in studs], ...]}.

rise.description: fill: plates between layers. 1 for plates, which is the default; 3 for courses of bricks.

seed.description: rock: which rock — each number leans and wanders its own way

shrink.description: fill: studs off each layer, taken half from each side, so the stack tapers as it rises. Must be even. 2 is a dome, 4 a steep cone, 0 a straight-sided hull, and -2 flares outward.

sideways.description: fill, prism: the share of its 1x2 bricks laid as two 1x1 bricks with a stud on the side, turned out and dressed with a tile, round tile, round plate or cheese slope on that stud, 0 to 0.5. For a wall one stud thick: a face built partly on its side, as real sets build them.

solids.description: shape: what it is made of, each an object naming one kind — {"loft": {...}}, {"extrude": {...}}, {"revolve": {...}}, {"box": {...}}, {"ellipsoid": {...}} or {"dome": {...}} — with its own "color" if it wants one (the last that holds a stud gives it its colour). Studs across and along, plates up, from at.

stack.description: round: what goes up the axis, bottom first, each square on the last. {"plates": N} a length of body ("color" a band of another colour, "diameter" wider or narrower, "spokes": 4 or 2 its top plate reaching a stud out with a "tile" on each reach — grid fins, gallery brackets, yard stubs); {"cones": 9 or 1} cones under a round plate ("cone_color") — nozzles, engine bells, lamps; {"technic": true, "struts": 0-4} a course with a pin hole out of each side and a Technic beam pinned on that many sides ("strut_color", "strut_length" in holes) — legs, stays; {"nose": cone, ogive, dome, point or flat} its top, and the end of the stack.

step.description: repeat: how far each copy moves, in studs and plates

storeys.description: prism: {"count": 2 to 8, "in": studs} — the courses split into storeys, each in studs smaller than the one below (its piers drawn in with it) and standing on a ledge two plates thick in the second tone, only the top storey's piers rising into horns: a tower that steps in as it rises, not a shaft. The reply says the top's radius (for add_rooms) and its summit's y.

surface.description: shape: curved slopes on its surface or straight ones; auto (the default) is curved if any solid is rounded.

thickness.description: prism: 2 (the default) closes the inside; 1 leaves slits at the corners

top.description: shape: tiles over its top (the default) or studs left showing.

top_color.description: shape: the colour of its top tiles and slopes, if not its own.

wall.description: fill: leave the middle out, this many studs in from every side. An ellipse with wall 1 is a round tube; a rectangle with wall 1 is a room's walls.

wheels.description: shape: a car on its own wheels — studs along x of each axle's middle, under a body laid along x 6, 8, 10 or 12 studs across. Each axle is a wheel and tyre each side on a Technic axle through Technic bricks, the body cut clear of each wheel's box and standing on the bricks (its underside 5 plates up or lower over them), so the car is one piece on its wheels. wheel_color is the rims' colour.

window_color.description: prism: the windows' colour (40, Trans-Brown, a dark slit, unless said)

windows.description: prism: a few narrow windows up every other face, a storey apart, dark slits unless window_color says; none unless said

axis.description: which way the hinge pin runs. z tips it left and right, x tips it forward and back, y swings it round.

degrees.description: how far it is turned about that pin. Any angle.

hinge.description: lean it on a hinge brick (3937 under 3938), put in for you: x, y, z are then where the hinge's base stands, the bricks in the section start at 0,0,0 on the hinge top's two studs (along the pin), and it turns about the hinge's own pin. A section leaning about x or z must turn on a joint; this is the one-line way.

name.description: what to call it, e.g. port nacelle

x.description: studs across, where this section's own origin sits

name: check_design

description: A section of how to design in this app, in full: "work" (the process: silhouette, features, detail), "rules", "shapes" (the patterns that lay a wall, a dome, a tower, a body and a head with its face), "subject" (what each kind of subject needs), "angle", "pins", "colour", "creative" and more. Read "shapes" before saying a shape.

section.description: work, rules, shapes, subject, real, colour, angle, coordinates, sideways, pins, big, look, good, beautiful, creative, changing, kind or art

name: read_guide

description: How a construction is actually made, in part numbers and coordinates, most of them as the LEGO Group built them in real sets. By what they are for — basics: half stud offset, face turned sideways, porthole or lamp, smooth diagonal, smooth top, taper; walls and stone: staggered wall, rough stone wall, weathered stone wall, corbelled wall walk, oversail on inverted slopes, stone corbel, balustrade, embossed brick wall; towers and columns: round tower, wide round tower, columns with capitals, stone column, turned wooden pillar; round bodies: round body, round body lying down, dome and cone cap, ring of cones under a round plate, spokes with tiles, curved skin panel, studs-out core, grille band, cone bell on round plates, round tip; faces and features: eye with a highlight, round face, beak or snout, ears or tufts, talons, headlamps and grille; machines and joints: struts pinned to a Technic course, two rounds pinned side by side, fin root on a Technic pin; angles: corner on a turntable, leaning on a hinge; roofs and spires: chimney, turret spire, roof ridge, striped awning; windows and doors: window in a wall, door in a wall, arched window, window with shutters, postern arch; rock and ground: fence, rock outcrop, rocky ground with plants, stone with ivy, cobbled path, staircase; plants: tree, planter, hedge with flowers, clipped hedge, leafy plant, flower bed; furniture and interiors: bed, bench, armchair, table, bookcase, fireplace, hearth, anvil, chest, potion shelf, dresser, sofa, four-poster bed, log pile; lights: lamp post, wall lantern, hanging lamp, bedside lamp, campfire; creative touches: lid or hatch raised on hinges, small creature, display stand with a nameplate. Ask before building one of these for the first time — a bracket's sideways stud is not at a whole number of plates, and the arithmetic is the part that goes wrong. Every one of them is checked against the same lattice your design is.

name.description: which one; a partial name will do

name: show_technique

description: How real LEGO® sets built a feature, found by what it is: the sub-assemblies of thousands of real sets (an owl's eye, a car's nose, a dragon's wing, a turret roof, a grille, a beak, a tree), each with a picture, its parts and colours, its size in studs, the set and modeller it is from, and an id for place_technique. Ask before inventing any feature of a face, a creature or a machine: a real designer's answer is better than a first guess. Name the subject too — "owl eye", "car nose" — and pieces from sets about it come first.

max_studs.description: the most studs wide or deep it may be; leave out for any size

query.description: the feature, and the subject it is on: "owl eye", "sports car front", "castle turret roof"

name: find_techniques

description: Parts by what they look like in a model, not by their catalogue name: "feather", "claw", "exhaust", "eyelid", "scales", "leaf". Each family of parts comes with what builders use it for and its commonest part numbers. search_parts finds a part you can name; this finds the one you can only describe.

query.description: what the part should read as

name: find_parts_like

description: Lay one of find_techniques' pieces into the model as the LEGO Group built it: every part where the set has it, turned a number of quarter turns about the upright and moved so its low corner is at x, y, z, in your colours if you say which of its colours become which. Parts cannot be scaled; pick a piece of the right size. Checked like any edit: it is refused, with the reason, if it overlaps the model or does not hold on. The answer lists the bricks as placed.

recolor.description: its colours to yours, by LDraw code: {"15": 4} makes its white parts red

x.description: studs across, to its low corner

y.description: plates up, to its low corner

z.description: studs deep, to its low corner

name: place_technique

description: Say what a feature is to be, once the app has laid a real set's piece for it where it goes (the whole review, each settle and saving hand the next feature with its piece laid and a picture): accept it — moved, turned or recoloured first if it needs it — ask for the next-best piece instead, reject it with a reason, or say you built it yourself. Saving waits until every feature listed in submit_design is settled.

feature.description: the feature, as listed in submit_design's features

move.description: accept, moved first: studs across and deep, plates up. The other of a pair moves the mirror way.

reason.description: a sentence: what is wrong with the piece here (to reject), or how you built it (built)

recolor.description: accept, recoloured first: its colours to yours by LDraw code, {"15": 1} makes its white blue

turn.description: accept, turned first: quarter turns on the spot

verdict.description: accept: keep the app's piece (adjusted by move, turn or recolor first, if given); next: take it off and lay the next-best piece; reject: take it off, with a reason, and build it your own way or leave it out; built: you built it yourself, and the app's piece comes off (accept keeps it)

name: settle_feature

description: How big the model should be, worked out before anything is placed. Give the real thing's longest dimension in metres and this answers with what it comes to in studs at each scale builders use, and which one is worth building at. Settle this first: everything after it depends on the proportions, and changing it later means moving the whole model.

longest_metres.description: how long the real thing is along its longest side. A guess within half is enough.

name: plan_scale

description: Pictures of a real thing, so you can build to what it looks like rather than to what you recall of it. Ask for this first for any subject that exists — a lighthouse, a tractor, a kingfisher, a particular building — and judge the proportions off the picture before you place a brick. The pictures come from Wikimedia Commons, which carries what is free to use: each is named and credited, and a famous ship from a film will not be there, so check what came back is the thing before building to it.

subject.description: what to look for, in the words you would use looking it up — "Fresnel lighthouse lantern room" rather than "lighthouse" when it is a detail you are after

name: find_reference

description:
What real LEGO® sets of this kind are actually built from — the parts they reach for far more often than sets in general, and the colours they use. Measured over fifteen thousand real sets, so it is what the LEGO Group's own designers did and not advice.

Call it for any subject that is a kind of set: a castle, a fire station, a spaceship, a train, a house, a tractor, a police car. A castle set is arch doors and lattice windows in tan and pearl gold; a fire station is trans-blue lights, taps and red; a spaceship is brackets, antennas, cones and inverted dishes in white and grey. That is the difference between a model of the thing and a model of bricks, and you cannot get it from the shape alone.

Give the plain word for the thing. Nothing matches a specific name.

With it comes our own best design of the nearest subject, as the design bench's judge scored it: how it was built, what it did best, and the faults to design out before you build.

subject.description: the kind of thing being built, in plain words — "fire station", "medieval castle", "spaceship"

name: how_real_sets_build_this

description: Where a part's studs are and the exact coordinates something sitting on each one would take. Ask about a brick that is already placed by its number, or about one you are considering by giving part and position. Use this rather than working out sideways positions yourself — a stud on the side of a brick is not at a whole number of plates and the arithmetic is easy to get wrong. It also draws the shape of any part that is not a plain box: which way a wedge plate tapers, which way a slope falls, where an arch is open. Ask before using one of those for the first time — a wedge put on backwards looks exactly like a wedge until you look at it.
name: attachment_points

description: A finishing pass over what is already built, wall by wall: plain bricks one stud wide (1x1 to 1x4) whose long face is open to the air, and the outer row of two-wide ones, are laid again in place as one structure per wall — ribs (a column of round plates on bricks with a stud on the side, every few studs), bands (a course of grille), panels (grille between the ribs, framed by a plain stud at each end and a plain course at each ledge, as 10237 Orthanc textures its black), grid (ribs and bands) or courses (round bricks, a recessed line) — in the wall's own colour, never a part at a time. A dark wall gets panels unasked; a light wall not given a style gets a scatter of dressed bricks (sideways) and masonry. The faces of a prism or a cluster too, in their own sections, and a model opened from a file. Done for you, in one call, checked like any edit.

face_color.description: the second tone: on every fifth rib and on bands; the rest is the wall's own colour, as a set dresses a black wall in black

masonry.description: a light wall given no style: share laid as masonry, 0 to 1; 0.25 if not said

sideways.description: a light wall given no style: share of its bricks turned out and dressed, 0 to 0.5; 0.15 if not said

style.description: how each wall is dressed, as one structure: panels on a dark wall if not said

texture.description: what panels and bands are laid in: grille (the default), masonry, logs (planking), round bricks (fluted) or headlight bricks

where.description: only bricks inside this box, in studs and plates, as look_at_model takes one; the whole model if left out

name: restyle_model

description: Floors and furnished rooms inside a building that already stands — a tower, a keep, a house — in one call, as a real set opens at the back onto them (10237 Orthanc: a library, Saruman's chamber, a dungeon, the palantír). Give the building's box (where) or, for a prism, the prism's own at, sides and radius (prism), and the floors bottom up, each a kind of room: library, study, bedchamber, hall, throne room, forge, armoury, dungeon, kitchen, lookout, palantir room, stair. Each floor is laid as plates and tiles held up on columns; each room is furnished from the worked examples real sets built — bookcases, a fireplace, an anvil, a four-poster bed, lamps, chests, barrels — against its walls and facing in, varied by the seed; stair: true climbs to the next floor. The shell is left as it is and the edit is checked like any other, so build it open at the back (a prism's open, or no back wall) for the rooms to be seen. This is where a real set's different pieces and colours are, and a solid shell has none of them.

room.description: what the room is, e.g. library or Saruman's chamber

stair.description: a stair from this floor up to the next

y.description: plates up, where its floor is laid; left out, floors stack up from the bottom

height.description: plates from one floor to the next when no y is said; 24 where the building is tall enough

prism.description: for a prism's inside: the same at, sides and radius (and thickness, if not 2) as the prism pattern, so the floors follow its faces

seed.description: another seed is another arrangement and other colours

where.description: the building, in studs and plates, as look_at_model takes a box: its walls and the inside between them. y_from is where the lowest floor goes if no floor says

name: add_rooms

description: Change what is already built without describing it again. Takes the numbers look_at_model prints beside each brick. Use this for any change to an existing model — moving a wall, recolouring a roof, taking a chimney off, adding a door — and only use submit_design when starting something new. Everything is checked together before any of it is applied, so a change that would not hold together changes nothing.

face.description: which way the studs point. Omit for up.

rot.description: quarter turns about the face direction, 0-3

section.description: the section this brick belongs to, if any. Its x, y and z are then that section's own coordinates, not the model's.

x.description: studs across, to the low corner. Tenths allowed.

y.description: plates up from the ground, to the low corner. Quarters allowed, for parts lying on their side.

z.description: studs deep, to the low corner. Tenths allowed.

assemblies.description: name a part of the model, as submit_design's assemblies do; one of the same name moves to the new box. Something meant to stand apart from the model — a display stand, a sign, a nameplate in front of it — must be named, its box holding it and none of the model: a piece apart that nothing names is a part that has come off, and fails.

name.description: what a person would call it, e.g. north-east tower

y_from.description: may be left out, for all of its height

repeat_section.description: say a section again somewhere else. One bay of a wall, repeated — rather than forty bays dictated.

axis.description: which way that pin runs. Defaults to the source section's.

degrees.description: turned this much further per copy, about the section's own origin. Put that origin at the centre of a tower and this walks the copies round it.

from.description: the name of a section that already has bricks in it

name.description: what to call the copies. They are numbered from 2.

times.description: how many copies to make, each one step further than the last

sections.description: add a section, or give one that already exists a new angle or position — which moves everything in it without naming a single brick.

axis.description: which way the hinge pin runs. z tips it left and right, x tips it forward and back, y swings it round.

degrees.description: how far it is turned about that pin. Any angle.

hinge.description: lean it on a hinge brick (3937 under 3938), put in for you: x, y, z are then where the hinge's base stands, the bricks in the section start at 0,0,0 on the hinge top's two studs (along the pin), and it turns about the hinge's own pin. A section leaning about x or z must turn on a joint; this is the one-line way.

name.description: what to call it, e.g. port nacelle

x.description: studs across, where this section's own origin sits

name: edit_model

description:
See what is already on the baseplate, in the same stud and plate coordinates you use. Call this first whenever the request is about what is there — adding to it, changing part of it, matching its colours or its height. You cannot see the model otherwise.

A large model will not fit in one reply. Give where= to list one section, or skip= to carry on from where the last listing stopped. The totals and the overall span are always for the whole model, whatever you ask for.

skip.description: How many matching bricks to pass over before listing, for walking through a model a section at a time.

where.description: Only the part of the model inside this box, in studs and plates. Any side may be left out.

name: look_at_model

description: Look at what is on the baseplate. This is the only way to see whether the thing you are building looks like the thing you were asked for. check_design tells you a model is legal; this tells you what it is.

from.description: which side to look from. corner is a three-quarter view and shows the shape best

where.description: Look closely at one part of the model rather than all of it, in studs and plates. The rest is still in the picture, just not filling it. On a big model a single assembly is a few dozen pixels across otherwise, which is not enough to judge its shape by.

name: view_model

description: Submit the finished model, with every part. It replaces everything on the baseplate that you put there — including anything you added with edit_model. If you have been building with edit_model, the model is already built: say so and stop, rather than submitting a list that is missing the additions.

assemblies.description: the parts of this model a person would name — the gatehouse, each tower, each run of wall, the keep — each a box in studs and plates. Once the model holds together and you have looked at it whole, each one is shown to you close up, on its own, to detail. A pass adds about as much to a big assembly as to a small one, so name them at about a hundred parts each: on a building, a floor's front is one and its sides another, the roof one and the sign on it another. A model that is one thing is one assembly.

name.description: what a person would call it, e.g. north-east tower

y_from.description: may be left out, for all of its height

face.description: which way the studs point. Omit for up.

rot.description: quarter turns about the face direction, 0-3

section.description: the section this brick belongs to, if any. Its x, y and z are then that section's own coordinates, not the model's.

x.description: studs across, to the low corner. Tenths allowed.

y.description: plates up from the ground, to the low corner. Quarters allowed, for parts lying on their side.

z.description: studs deep, to the low corner. Tenths allowed.

features.description: what the subject is known by, a few words each: an owl's facial disc, eyes, beak, ear tufts, wings, talons; a car's wheel arches, headlamps, grille, windscreen, spoiler — and where each goes: x, y, z on the model's surface and the way it faces out (one of a pair; the other is mirrored). Once the shape stands and you have looked at it whole, each comes back to you in turn with the best real set's piece for it laid there by the app, to accept, adjust or reject with settle_feature.

facing.description: the way it faces out; the front is +z

floor.description: what it stands on. "none" for anything that is picked up and played with or stood on a shelf — a vehicle, a ship, a figure, a creature, a spacecraft: a set like that has no plate in the box. "baseplate" for a scene, a diorama, a building on its lot, a landscape: a real baseplate, sized to it, goes in the box as the first part of the build — build on it, never lay ground plates of your own under the model as well. "grid" for neither. Say in the description which you chose and why; the person can change it.

floor_colour.description: a baseplate's colour, from the colours baseplates come in: Green, Bright Green, Dark Green, Tan, Dark Tan, Light Bluish Grey, Dark Bluish Grey, Sand Green, Blue, White, Black. Grass is green, a road or a yard grey, sand or a desert tan, water blue, snow white.

about.description: mirror: which way the line runs

at.description: mirror: the line to reflect about, in studs. fill, round: where the footprint's low corner sits, as {x, y, z} (a round lying along x or z: the low end of it, on the ground).

axis.description: round: y stands it up (the default); x or z lays it along that axis on the ground — a boiler, a fuselage, a hull, a log

band_color.description: fill with rise 3, prism: a course in this colour every eight, a string course where a storey's ledge is. A black wall gets dark bluish grey bands unless mix_color or this says otherwise.

bands.description: shape: [{"from": plates, "to": plates, "color"}] — a waterline, a stripe, a belly, by height.

beside.description: round: more rounds standing round this one, touching it, pinned where their Technic courses meet (start both stacks the same, each with a technic course at one height): {"count": 2 or 4, "diameter", "color", "stack"}. Boosters on a core, twin funnels, a cluster of silos.

box.description: shape: {"from": [x, y, z], "size": [across, plates up, deep], "round": studs its plan corners are rounded by, "chamfer": studs they are cut by, "edge": studs its top edges are rounded by}.

bricks.description: repeat: what to repeat. mirror: what to reflect, if not everything so far.

face.description: which way the studs point. Omit for up.

rot.description: quarter turns about the face direction, 0-3

section.description: the section this brick belongs to, if any. Its x, y and z are then that section's own coordinates, not the model's.

x.description: studs across, to the low corner. Tenths allowed.

y.description: plates up from the ground, to the low corner. Quarters allowed, for parts lying on their side.

z.description: studs deep, to the low corner. Tenths allowed.

color.description: fill, rock: the colour (rock: 72 if not said)

courses.description: studs_out: how many rows, each four plates tall; prism: how many courses of bricks, three plates each (with piers, left out for a display model's proportions, 3.3 times as tall as wide)

cuts.description: shape: solids taken away, said the same way: a cockpit, a doorway; "keep": true keeps the cut clear of every part.

diameter.description: round: studs across — the sizes round parts come in (at is the low corner of its square)

dome.description: shape: an ellipsoid's top half, said the same way.

door.description: prism: an arched door at the foot of the face looking +z, two studs wide and six courses tall, for a stair to lead up to; true unless said with piers, false unless said without

dress.description: studs_out: what every side stud carries — a mix (the default), flat tiles for a smooth panel, round plates as rivets, round tiles as portholes, or lights (round tiles in a transparent face_color): a band of detail along a hull, a boiler, a wall

edge_color.description: fill: a second colour for the outside stud of every layer — hull plating, a trim, a kerb.

ellipsoid.description: shape: {"centre": [x, y, z], "radii": [studs across, plates up, studs deep]}.

extrude.description: shape: {"along": "x" or "z", "from": studs across, "width": studs, "profile": [[studs along, plates up], ...] its top seen from the side, "under": the same for its underside (0 unless said), "round": studs its top edges are rounded by}.

face.description: shape: a face laid on a curved side, studs out — {"facing": "+z", "x", "y", "z": its middle, "across": 4, 6 or 8, "color": the disc, "rim": the plate behind it, "eyes": the iris, "beak": its colour or -1}: a round plate disc on side studs, two 2 x 2 round eyes with printed eye tiles, a beak.

face_color.description: studs_out: the colour of what is laid on the side studs

facing.description: studs_out: which way the face looks

layers.description: fill: how many of the footprint, stacked up

loft.description: shape: {"along": "x" or "z", "centre": studs across (half the widest unless said), "sections": [{"at": studs along, "width": studs, "height": plates, "bottom": plates, "round": 0 a box to 1 an ellipse, "keel": 0 to 1, how far its lower half narrows to a V, "offset": studs across}, ...]} — the section between each two is in between; width 0 at an end is a point.

masonry.description: fill: the share of its 1x2 and 1x4 bricks laid as masonry bricks (98283, 15533), stonework facing away from the middle, 0 to 1. For a wall one stud thick.

mix.description: fill: the share in mix_color, up to 0.5; 0.15 if not said.

mix_color.description: fill, rock: a second colour through some of its bricks, chosen by where they are, the same every time — a weathered wall. Real castle walls are 9-19% their second grey.

open.description: prism: faces left out at the back, so the rooms inside show; with piers, any number opens the core's whole back, the piers there left closed

panels.description: shape: its straight sides as tiles on bricks with side studs every other course (true, the default), or plain bricks (false).

pattern.description: repeat: the bricks again, stepped each time. mirror: everything so far, reflected about a line — build one side and mirror it rather than writing both. fill: a footprint tiled with the largest plates that fit, or with rise 3 a wall of short bricks in a running bond — and with layers, a shrink and a wall it is a dome, a cone, a hull, a tube or a bowl in one object. rock: a crag in one object — courses stepping in unevenly towards a peak off the middle, faced with slopes, cheese slopes, pebbles and bare ledges in two greys; a different seed is a different rock. studs_out: a face built sideways in one object — courses of 1x1 bricks with a side stud, tied by plates, each stud carrying a tile, round tile, round plate or cheese slope laid on its side; the arithmetic of where a side stud is, done for you. prism: a many-sided shaft in one object — a tower, a pier, a turret of 5 to 16 sides, each face a bonded wall turned to its angle about the middle (at is the middle), grooved where the faces meet. round: anything round in section, in one object — a column, a rocket stage, a lighthouse, a silo, a boiler, a fuselage, a tree trunk — of the round parts sets use at each diameter (round bricks, cylinder halves, corner rounds tied by round plates), colour bands, cones, Technic struts and spokes up its stack, ending in a nose; upright or lying along x or z. shape: a body that is not a box, said as solids — a loft through cross-sections, an extruded side profile, a revolve, a box with rounded or cut corners and edges, an ellipsoid or dome — less any cuts, laid in the parts a builder would choose: bricks and plates inside, slopes and curved slopes fitted to the surface's fall, inverted slopes under it, wedge plates on a diagonal edge, round parts where a section is round, a side that curves up and down laid on its side on side studs, tiles on top, one half and its mirror; a car's body, a hull, a fuselage, an animal's body. Another shape standing on it keeps its studs there.

piers.description: prism: faceted piers clustered round it, each a prism of its own built against the core, with a cleft between each two — a tower like Orthanc in one object. The core is capped with a summit two plates thick at y + 3 x courses, and piers taller than the core rise past it as horns: blades of plates on their side, cut by wedge plates, sweeping out and back in to a point (the reply says where the tips are).

courses.description: how tall, in courses of three plates; more than the core's for horns (a fifth more; a blade rises at least two and a half times its width)

flare.description: blade: studs its sweep reaches out (half its width)

horns.description: what piers taller than the core rise into: a blade (the default, as set 10237 builds Orthanc's), a square spire stepping in to a point, or flat, a turret's cap

out.description: studs from the core's middle to each pier's (set into the core by its wall's thickness)

radius.description: studs from a pier's middle to the outside of its faces (two thirds of the core's; smaller than keeps faces two studs wide at its sides, it is laid at that and said)

turn.description: degrees round from +z to the first pier (between two faces, so there is a cleft front and back)

plinth.description: prism: {"steps": 1 to 4, "out": studs, "stair": true, "rock": true} — the tower raised on square terraces stepping down from its foot, two courses each, their tops tiled in the second tone up to its faces, with a stair cut into the front (+z) up to its door's level, and crags in its dark tones rising against it at their corners and sides (rock: false for none). The reply says the tower's foot (and add_rooms' y).

radius.description: prism: studs from the middle to the outside of a face

revolve.description: shape: {"axis": "y", "x" or "z", "centre": [x, y, z], "profile": [[along it (plates up y, studs along x or z), radius in studs], ...]}.

rise.description: fill: plates between layers. 1 for plates, which is the default; 3 for courses of bricks.

seed.description: rock: which rock — each number leans and wanders its own way

shrink.description: fill: studs off each layer, taken half from each side, so the stack tapers as it rises. Must be even. 2 is a dome, 4 a steep cone, 0 a straight-sided hull, and -2 flares outward.

sideways.description: fill, prism: the share of its 1x2 bricks laid as two 1x1 bricks with a stud on the side, turned out and dressed with a tile, round tile, round plate or cheese slope on that stud, 0 to 0.5. For a wall one stud thick: a face built partly on its side, as real sets build them.

solids.description: shape: what it is made of, each an object naming one kind — {"loft": {...}}, {"extrude": {...}}, {"revolve": {...}}, {"box": {...}}, {"ellipsoid": {...}} or {"dome": {...}} — with its own "color" if it wants one (the last that holds a stud gives it its colour). Studs across and along, plates up, from at.

stack.description: round: what goes up the axis, bottom first, each square on the last. {"plates": N} a length of body ("color" a band of another colour, "diameter" wider or narrower, "spokes": 4 or 2 its top plate reaching a stud out with a "tile" on each reach — grid fins, gallery brackets, yard stubs); {"cones": 9 or 1} cones under a round plate ("cone_color") — nozzles, engine bells, lamps; {"technic": true, "struts": 0-4} a course with a pin hole out of each side and a Technic beam pinned on that many sides ("strut_color", "strut_length" in holes) — legs, stays; {"nose": cone, ogive, dome, point or flat} its top, and the end of the stack.

step.description: repeat: how far each copy moves, in studs and plates

storeys.description: prism: {"count": 2 to 8, "in": studs} — the courses split into storeys, each in studs smaller than the one below (its piers drawn in with it) and standing on a ledge two plates thick in the second tone, only the top storey's piers rising into horns: a tower that steps in as it rises, not a shaft. The reply says the top's radius (for add_rooms) and its summit's y.

surface.description: shape: curved slopes on its surface or straight ones; auto (the default) is curved if any solid is rounded.

thickness.description: prism: 2 (the default) closes the inside; 1 leaves slits at the corners

top.description: shape: tiles over its top (the default) or studs left showing.

top_color.description: shape: the colour of its top tiles and slopes, if not its own.

wall.description: fill: leave the middle out, this many studs in from every side. An ellipse with wall 1 is a round tube; a rectangle with wall 1 is a room's walls.

wheels.description: shape: a car on its own wheels — studs along x of each axle's middle, under a body laid along x 6, 8, 10 or 12 studs across. Each axle is a wheel and tyre each side on a Technic axle through Technic bricks, the body cut clear of each wheel's box and standing on the bricks (its underside 5 plates up or lower over them), so the car is one piece on its wheels. wheel_color is the rims' colour.

window_color.description: prism: the windows' colour (40, Trans-Brown, a dark slit, unless said)

windows.description: prism: a few narrow windows up every other face, a storey apart, dark slits unless window_color says; none unless said

axis.description: which way that pin runs. Defaults to the source section's.

degrees.description: turned this much further per copy, about the section's own origin. Put that origin at the centre of a tower and this walks the copies round it.

from.description: the name of a section that already has bricks in it

name.description: what to call the copies. They are numbered from 2.

times.description: how many copies to make, each one step further than the last

axis.description: which way the hinge pin runs. z tips it left and right, x tips it forward and back, y swings it round.

degrees.description: how far it is turned about that pin. Any angle.

hinge.description: lean it on a hinge brick (3937 under 3938), put in for you: x, y, z are then where the hinge's base stands, the bricks in the section start at 0,0,0 on the hinge top's two studs (along the pin), and it turns about the hinge's own pin. A section leaning about x or z must turn on a joint; this is the one-line way.

name.description: what to call it, e.g. port nacelle

x.description: studs across, where this section's own origin sits

sketch.description: true for a sketch: massing only, under 150 parts, checked and pictured but not built. Three are made to choose between before the full design, each a different idea: in silhouette, proportion or approach.

name: submit_design

description: Stand a minifigure in the model, made from real parts in their real places: who lives in it, guards it, works in it. Add them once the model is built — submitting a whole new design replaces them. Each slot takes a part number or a few words matched against the names of the parts made for it ("wizard hat", "long beard", "robe", "staff"); leave a slot out for a plain one. It stands on whatever is highest under its feet, two studs side by side, and is refused if something is in the way. Its parts are not counted in the model's variety, as a set's figures are not.

accessory.description: what it holds in its right hand

accessory_left.description: what it holds in its left hand

arms.description: plain, printed sleeves, or another arm ("skeleton", "wing")

back.description: airtanks, a backpack, a quiver, wings, or left out

colors.description: LDraw colour codes by slot: headwear, hat_extra, head, neck, back, cape, torso, arms, hands, hips, hipwear, legs, footwear, accessory, accessory_left. A printed torso brings arm and hand colours of its own.

facing.description: which way its face looks: +z, the default, is towards the front view

footwear.description: flippers, skis, skates, or left out

hands.description: plain, or a hook, boxing gloves, a prosthetic

hat_extra.description: a visor, plume or feathers fixed onto the headgear

hips.description: a printed belt or sash, or left out

hipwear.description: a skirt, a tail or a belt over the hips

legs.description: plain, printed, "short" for a child, a wooden leg, a mermaid tail

name.description: who it is; the name of its sub-model in the saved file

neck.description: armour, a scarf, a beard, a life jacket, or left out

torso.description: what is printed on the chest; an odd body (a battle droid, a skeleton) brings its own head, arms and legs

x.description: studs: the first of the two studs it stands on

y.description: plates: the height of the floor it stands on, which a room or a balcony with anything over it needs; left out, it stands on whatever is highest at that spot

name: add_minifig

description: Make a part the LEGO Group has not made, when no real part will do: search_parts first, and use a real one if there is one. Either a new part of a family at any size — a 1 x 7 brick, a bracket with a 3 x 2 upright, a Technic brick 1 x 9, a brick with studs on two sides — or a real part changed: from="3700" with across 6, from="3062b" without its studs, from="3003" with a corner cut out. It is checked as a person's part is (sizes the system has, walls 1.6 mm, studs on the grid) and refused with the reason if it cannot be made. Made, it is a part like any other: put its number in check_design, edit_model or submit_design, and a saved model carries it. Its studs, holes and pins are found as a real part's are, so it clutches and pins as they do.

across.description: studs along X: a brick's length; a slope's, bracket's or curved slope's width along its face or upright; a Technic brick's length. With from: the new length.

angle.description: slope, inverted: one of the named angles of LEGO® slopes, which sets run and plates as the real part has them

cut.description: with from: a box to cut out of the part — a corner, a notch, a step — in studs from its low x and low z (its left and back) and plates up from its bottom; the cut faces are closed and a wall put back where it opens the part's hollow underside.

deep.description: studs along Z: a brick's width; a slope's depth from back to foot; a bracket's plate depth. With from: the new width.

family.description: for a new part: brick (also plates and tiles: plates 1, studs false), slope, curved (a curved slope), inverted (slope), round, bracket (a plate with an upright whose studs face forward), technic (a 1 x N brick with a hole between every two studs)

from.description: instead of a family: a real part's number to change, keeping everything not changed as the LEGO Group made it. Longer, wider and taller repeat a slice of it; a part with no slice that repeats (a 1 x 1, a round brick across) is refused.

name.description: what to call it; left out, it is named as LDraw names its parts

plates.description: height in plates, 3 to a brick (a bracket is 1, a Technic brick 3). With from: the new height.

rise.description: bracket: the upright's height in studs

run.description: slope, inverted, curved: the rows the face falls over, from the front; the rest are flat with studs

sides.description: brick: the sides with studs on them, letters of fblr: f is the +z face (the front), b -z, l -x, r +x; studs 10 LDU under the top and every stud down. Needs 3 plates or more.

studs.description: a new part: true for studs on top (the default), false for a tile. With from: "keep", "none" to take them off, "fill" to put them on wherever the top is flat.

way.description: bracket: whether the upright hangs down from the plate's front edge or stands up from it

name: make_part

description:
Lay a picture as a LEGO® Art set is laid — 31212 The Milky Way, 31208 The Great Wave, 31213 Mona Lisa — on 16 x 16 panels joined underneath into one piece: square tiles merged where it is flat, 1 x 1 round tiles for texture, quarter circles along curved contours, stars in trans-clear, glow-in-the-dark, pearl and metallic set a plate proud, and the subject raised on stacked plates with cheese slopes. Use this, not submit_design, whenever a mosaic, a picture in bricks, wall art or something like a LEGO® Art set is asked for. It replaces what is on the baseplate.
The picture is the one the person chose (look_at_picture shows it). With none, draw it yourself as svg: one stud is one pixel, so big simple shapes in flat colours, like a poster.
You decide what a designer of LEGO® Art sets decides, and the app reads everything you leave out off the picture: the panels and the crop; regions over the picture, each with its texture, its relief (the subject raised, the background flat), whether contours run in it and whether its points of light are stars and in what finish; single stars put exactly where you want them; a palette to keep to. Coordinates are fractions of the picture, 0 to 1 from its top left. Later regions lie over earlier ones and change only what they say, so start with the whole picture and work inward. A plan that cannot be laid is refused with every fault named.
The answer is the picture as laid, face on, and what it is made of. Look at it as a person would from across a room, and call make_art again with the plan changed if it does not read as the subject.

base_colour.description: the panels' LDraw colour, which shows between round tiles: usually the darkest of the background

depth.description: how high relief read off the picture rises where no region gives one; 0 keeps it flat there. Default 3.

palette.description: LDraw colour codes to lay it in, as a set keeps to a dozen or so. Leave it out for all of them.

panels.description: [across, down], 1 to 6 each; a panel is 16 studs, 12.8 cm. down 0 keeps the picture's proportions. A large set is 4 to 6 across.

points.description: single stars put by hand (default 1 x 1 trans-clear). A sky like 31212's has dozens, of varied size and finish

at.description: [x, y], fractions of the picture from its top left

finish.description: a star's finish: trans-clear, glow, pearl-white, pearl-grey, pearl-gold, metallic-gold, metallic-silver, trans-light-blue, trans-medium-blue, trans-dark-blue, trans-yellow, trans-orange, trans-red, trans-purple, or an LDraw colour code

size.description: 1 (default): a 1 x 1 round tile; 2: a 2 x 2 round tile, for the few brightest

colour.description: lay the whole region in this one LDraw colour, whatever the picture has there

contours.description: curved edges inside it laid in quarter-circle tiles (default true)

rx.description: half-width, a fraction of the picture's width

ry.description: half-height, also a fraction of the WIDTH, so rx = ry is a circle

everything.description: the whole picture; put it first

finish.description: a star's finish: trans-clear, glow, pearl-white, pearl-grey, pearl-gold, metallic-gold, metallic-silver, trans-light-blue, trans-medium-blue, trans-dark-blue, trans-yellow, trans-orange, trans-red, trans-purple, or an LDraw colour code

name.description: what it is: sky, core, the crest

items.description: [x, y], fractions of the picture from its top left

relief.description: plates it stands above the panel. The background 0; the subject raised in terraces, an outer region 1 and an inner 2 or 3; cheese slopes are laid on the way up

stars.description: whether points of light the picture has here become stars in a finish (default true). False on a subject whose highlights are not stars

texture.description: round: 1 x 1 round tiles, the theme's texture, for what is busy or soft (a star field, foam, cloud, hair, fur); smooth: square tiles merged into long ones, for flat colour (sky, a wall, a plain ground); picture: round where the picture is busy and smooth where it is flat

svg.description: the picture, drawn, when the person has not chosen one: a whole <svg> with a viewBox in the panels' proportions (0 0 96 48 for 6 x 3 panels, a unit a stud) and a rect filling it as the background. Leave it out to use their picture.

name: make_art

description: The picture the person chose to make into Brick Art, as they gave it, with its size in pixels. Look at it before writing a make_art plan from it. When there is none it says so: draw one in make_art's svg.
name: look_at_picture

description: What the person has selected in Brickworks — the parts they mean by "this", "these" or "the selected": each by number with where it stands, their box, the sub-assembly they are in, the room a change about them may use, how the joints round them stand, and pictures with them picked out, close up and in the whole model. Call it whenever a request is about part of the model, then change that part with edit_selection.
name: selection

description: Change the selected parts as edit_model does — take off, paint, move, put down — keeping to the selection's room: a change that reaches outside it is refused whole, and everything else in the model stays where it is. It is checked as any design is, so a change that would not hold together or leaves a part loose changes nothing, and the refusal says, part by part, what each ran into or why nothing holds it, and the nearest place it fits and holds. check_only=true tries a change without making it. Other copies of the sub-assembly follow the change. One undo takes the request back. For more room, give room= and why=: the person is asked first.

face.description: which way the studs point. Omit for up.

rot.description: quarter turns about the face direction, 0-3

section.description: the section this brick belongs to, if any. Its x, y and z are then that section's own coordinates, not the model's.

x.description: studs across, to the low corner. Tenths allowed.

y.description: plates up from the ground, to the low corner. Quarters allowed, for parts lying on their side.

z.description: studs deep, to the low corner. Tenths allowed.

assemblies.description: name a part of the model, as submit_design's assemblies do; one of the same name moves to the new box. Something meant to stand apart from the model — a display stand, a sign, a nameplate in front of it — must be named, its box holding it and none of the model: a piece apart that nothing names is a part that has come off, and fails.

name.description: what a person would call it, e.g. north-east tower

y_from.description: may be left out, for all of its height

check_only.description: try the change without making it: says whether it would be applied, or why not and the nearest place each refused part fits and holds

repeat_section.description: say a section again somewhere else. One bay of a wall, repeated — rather than forty bays dictated.

axis.description: which way that pin runs. Defaults to the source section's.

degrees.description: turned this much further per copy, about the section's own origin. Put that origin at the centre of a tower and this walks the copies round it.

from.description: the name of a section that already has bricks in it

name.description: what to call the copies. They are numbered from 2.

times.description: how many copies to make, each one step further than the last

room.description: more room than the selection gives, in studs and plates, when the change cannot be made inside it. The person is asked in the app, and the change goes ahead only if they say yes.

sections.description: add a section, or give one that already exists a new angle or position — which moves everything in it without naming a single brick.

axis.description: which way the hinge pin runs. z tips it left and right, x tips it forward and back, y swings it round.

degrees.description: how far it is turned about that pin. Any angle.

hinge.description: lean it on a hinge brick (3937 under 3938), put in for you: x, y, z are then where the hinge's base stands, the bricks in the section start at 0,0,0 on the hinge top's two studs (along the pin), and it turns about the hinge's own pin. A section leaning about x or z must turn on a joint; this is the one-line way.

name.description: what to call it, e.g. port nacelle

x.description: studs across, where this section's own origin sits

why.description: why the change needs that room, in a sentence the person reads

name: edit_selection

description: Where the selected parts can take another part: every open stud, anti-stud (the hollow underneath that takes a stud), side stud, pin hole, bar and clip, grouped by the way it faces, each with the part that carries it and where it is in the coordinates edit_selection takes (a section's own, for parts laid turned), and a picture with the free ones numbered. Give part= (and color=) and it seats that part on them and tries each against the model as it stands: what comes back fits and holds, to put in edit_selection's add as it is. toward= puts first the points facing that way (out: away from the model's middle, for spikes or detail on an outer face); near= {x, y, z} those nearest a place.

color.description: its LDraw colour; the colour of the part it goes on when omitted

limit.description: how many placements of part to give; 8 when omitted

part.description: a part to seat on the open points, e.g. 49668

name: where_to_attach

description: Choose one of the three sketches made with submit_design "sketch": true. It goes on the baseplate as the massing the full design is built from, and the other two are dropped. Then design the whole model from it, and submit_design that without sketch.
name: choose_sketch

description: Look a built model over the way Brickworks' own designer does after a design stands: with no assembly, the whole model measured against real LEGO® sets of its size and kind — shapes, colours, the one-off pieces, how coarse — and what to check it for; with an assembly named in submit_design, that one close up, measured, with the parts real sets of the kind use that it has none of; with a feature (eyes, beak, wheel arches, grille), the best real set's piece for it laid by the app where it goes, with a picture, to settle with settle_feature; with creative, the creative pass — three touches proposed for this subject and the best one or two added. Call it after submit_design, then once per feature, then once per assembly, working each before the next, then creative last.

assembly.description: an assembly's name as given in submit_design; omit for the whole model

creative.description: true for the creative pass, once the features and assemblies have had their turns

feature.description: a feature the subject is known by, as listed in submit_design's features

name: review_model

description: Take everything off the baseplate and start from bare ground. Do this before building something new, or the new thing is built into the old one.
name: clear_model

description: Write what is on the baseplate to an LDraw .ldr file in this app's models, where its Open finds it and other LDraw tools can read it. A name, not a path; it will not write over a model the person saved.

name.description: the file's name, such as orthanc.ldr

name: save_model

description: Choose what the model stands on, as View, Floor does: a baseplate (studs across and deep, in eights from 8 to 192, in a colour baseplates come in), a grid floor with no plate, or none — a vehicle stands on a table, a scene on a baseplate in its ground's colour. part_of_model=true makes the baseplate a part of the model: counted, saved, step 1 of the booklet. Nothing built moves. With nothing given it says what it is now.

across.description: studs along x; 16, 32 and 48 are the square ones the LEGO Group sells

colour.description: LDraw code: 2 Green, 10 Bright Green, 288 Dark Green, 19 Tan, 28 Dark Tan, 71 Light Bluish Grey, 72 Dark Bluish Grey, 378 Sand Green, 1 Blue, 15 White, 0 Black, 7 Light Grey

deep.description: studs along z; the same as across when omitted

name: set_floor

description: The model's build steps, the order the booklet and the timeline follow, as Edit, Build steps changes them. op "list" (the default) gives them with the part numbers in each; "next" or "prev" moves bricks= a step later or earlier; "new" makes a new step of bricks=; "earlier", "later", "merge" (with the next) and "delete" act on step=, a number from the list. A model with no steps of its own is given the worked-out ones first, in the same undo step.

bricks.description: part numbers from look_at_model, for next, prev and new

from.description: list from this step; 1 when omitted

step.description: a step's number, for earlier, later, merge and delete

name: edit_steps

description: Lay a hose, tube, string or chain, as Build, Hose, tube or chain does: kind ribbed_hose, pneumatic_tube, flex_hose or flex_axle between two parts' pin holes, axles or pins; string between two studs; chain or tread round sprockets= (two or more gears in one plane). The real length that fits is chosen, and it bends no tighter than the real one can. It goes in as one sub-assembly, named in the answer; item= that name lays it again between new ends.

x.description: studs: the connector nearest this, when the part has several

item.description: a hose already laid, by its name in an earlier answer

sprockets.description: part numbers of the gears a chain or tread goes round

x.description: studs: the connector nearest this, when the part has several

name: lay_flex

description: Swing a part about its joint, as Build, Pose does: a sub-assembly on a hinge, a turntable or a clip on a bar. With no joint it lists them, numbered, with the angle each is at. joint= (number or name) and degrees= (from where it was built, -180 to 180) swings it as far as it has room; the answer says where it stopped if something is in the way.

joint.description: its number or name in the list

name: pose_model

description: Animate the model as Build, Pose's keys do: poses at moments, played smoothly between (an arm raised over two seconds and lowered again, doors opening), the model turned round once as well if asked, and rendered as an animation (a WebP, and an MP4 where ffmpeg is installed) where Render saves. keys: [{"t": seconds, "angles": {joint: degrees}}], joints by number or name from pose_model's list. Rendering needs the app in a window; render=false only sets the keys, for the person to play.

angles.description: joint (number or name) -> degrees from where it was built

turntable.description: turn the model round once over it

name: animate_model

description: Take back the last change to the model, as Edit, Undo does — yours or the person's — or steps= of them. redo=true puts back what was undone. The answer names what was undone and what is next.
name: undo

description: The person's saved models and the examples that come with the app, with their part counts; name= opens one in place of what is on the baseplate, as File, Open does. Opening cannot be undone, so it is refused while the model has changes not saved, unless discard_changes=true.

name.description: a model's name from the list

name: open_model

description: The model's parts, as Build, Parts list shows them: by part and colour, with counts and LEGO® element ids. which="need" measures it against the person's collection (My collection): how much they own and what they are short of; which="buildable" says which of their saved models their collection builds.
name: parts_list

description: Render the model as File, Render does: a picture, or a turntable (a WebP and, where ffmpeg is installed, an MP4), on a studio sweep with soft shadows. quality quick, good or best (good for a picture, quick for a turntable when omitted); size 720p, 1080p, 4k or square; view hero, front, side, back, low or top. Saved where Render saves, and a picture comes back with the answer. Needs the app in a window.
name: render_model

description: Write the model out as File, Export does, where Export writes (the Downloads folder; a download on the web): format ldraw (.ldr, or .mpd with its sub-models, with its build steps), studio (a BrickLink Studio .io), a 3D file at real size — glb (one file: Blender, three.js, AR; any size of model), gltf (the same as text), obj (with an .mtl of its colours) or stl (one mesh in mm, Z up, to 3D print); obj and stl hold every triangle and are capped — picture (.png), bricklink (a wanted list), rebrickable (a parts list .csv), or instructions (the building instructions as a booklet to print, which takes a while on a big model).
name: export_model
